study_sequence.directive: Define what makes a problem a computing problem and write a clear problem statement that specifies inputs, required outputs, and constraints at an appropriate level of precision.
Explain abstraction as the practice of hiding unnecessary detail and build/choose a model (data representation and simplified view) that preserves what matters for solving the problem.
Describe an algorithm as a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps and produce a candidate algorithm for a stated problem (e.g., in pseudocode or structured English).
Use decomposition, pattern recognition, and abstraction to transform a complex problem into parts and outline how those parts can be recombined into an algorithmic solution.
State what it means for an algorithm to be correct and discuss efficiency at a high level (time/space) as a tradeoff that matters when selecting among solutions.
Given an example from a non-CS field, identify the role of data, models, and algorithms and articulate how computing methods support discovery, decision-making, or automation in that domain.

Explain computational thinking as a systematic way to formulate problems and solution approaches so they can be executed by a computer (or by a precise procedure). Distinguish it from simply “coding” by emphasizing problem formulation and methodical solution design.

Show how to break a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts with clear inputs/outputs for each part. Provide at least one worked example of a decomposition that supports later solution construction.

Describe how to identify repeated structures across subproblems or instances and use those similarities to generalize a reusable approach. Include an example that demonstrates moving from specific cases to a generalized method.

Define abstraction as selecting relevant details and suppressing irrelevant ones to build a model suitable for computation. Demonstrate how an abstraction/model enables a clearer algorithmic solution.

Teach learners to express a solution as an unambiguous, ordered sequence of steps, including how data flows through those steps. Provide at least one algorithm written in clear pseudocode or structured steps.

Explain how to assess whether a designed procedure solves the intended problem (correctness) and how resource use (time/space) may vary among alternatives. Include a comparison scenario where a more efficient approach is favored under constraints.
Define an ADT as a specification of data plus allowed operations, separating interface from implementation, and show how this enables reasoning about algorithms independent of representation.
Describe how solving a computing problem involves jointly selecting/defining data representations and algorithms, and articulate the tradeoffs that drive those choices.
Introduce the main families (arrays/lists, stacks/queues, sets/maps, trees, graphs) at a high level and describe the kinds of problems each is suited for in terms of operations supported.
List common operations (access, search, insert, delete, traverse) and describe how to evaluate their costs under a stated model (e.g., counting primitive steps and memory use).
Explain what a data structure is and why choosing one changes the time/space cost of operations and the overall efficiency of algorithms that use it.
State that algorithms must be correct but are also judged by efficiency, and frame data structures as a primary lever for meeting efficiency constraints without changing problem meaning.

Explain that models of computation come with resource measures (time/steps, space/memory) used to compare algorithms. Relate these measures to earlier correctness/efficiency tradeoffs and to choosing representations/approaches.

Define what a model of computation is and what questions it helps answer (what can be computed, and with what resource costs). Contrast models by the kinds of problems/algorithms they can express and analyze.

Explain finite-state computation (states, transitions, input consumption) and what it can/cannot compute compared with more powerful models. Provide a simple example of modeling a system as a state machine.

Introduce lambda calculus (functions, application, substitution) as an alternative model of computation. Explain at a high level how functional evaluation computes results and why this model matters for language design and reasoning.

Describe the stored-program idea and the major components (processor, memory, instructions/data in memory, I/O) and how execution proceeds step-by-step. Explain why this model underlies mainstream low-level languages and machine execution.

Present the Turing machine as a reference model for general computation and use it to articulate the idea of computability/limits. Connect the model to the concept of algorithms as precise procedures and to reasoning about what problems have algorithmic solutions.

Explain the CPU’s internal organization at a high level (control unit, ALU, registers, program counter) and walk through the fetch–decode–execute cycle for an instruction. Clarify what state changes (register/memory) occur across the cycle.

Differentiate where instructions live versus where data lives at runtime, and how each is moved/used (registers ↔ memory ↔ I/O). Provide examples of common data movement patterns (load/store, memory-mapped I/O at a conceptual level).

Summarize how I/O devices and secondary storage are organized and accessed (controllers, device interfaces, block vs. stream devices at a conceptual level). Explain why I/O and storage are slower than CPU/register access and what that implies for program behavior.

Identify common bottlenecks (CPU vs. memory vs. I/O) and articulate basic tradeoffs in system organization that affect performance. Provide a qualitative comparison (not detailed math) of relative latencies/bandwidths and how they constrain throughput.

Describe the major hardware components (CPU, main memory, persistent storage, and I/O devices) and explain how they communicate via interconnects (buses/controllers). Include a simple block-diagram-level account of data/control flow between components during program execution.

State the stored-program idea and relate it to a computer system organization where instructions and data are encoded as bits and stored in memory. Connect this organization to how algorithms become executable programs on real machines.
Describe how an OS hides hardware details behind simpler interfaces (the 'virtual machine' view), and give concrete examples of abstractions such as processes, virtual memory, and files.
Explain the distinction between the kernel and user programs, why privileged execution exists, and how protection/isolation supports safe sharing of hardware among programs.
Explain what an operating system is and why it exists, emphasizing its dual role as (1) an abstraction layer over hardware and (2) a resource manager for running programs.
Define OS-provided services from an application’s perspective and introduce system calls as the programmatic boundary between user programs and privileged OS functionality.
Summarize common OS structures and categories (e.g., monolithic vs microkernel; general-purpose vs embedded/real-time) and connect each to the design goals it prioritizes.
State which resources the OS manages (CPU time, memory, storage, I/O devices) and outline the goals and tensions in allocation (efficiency, fairness, responsiveness).
Explain how a language defines order of execution (sequencing, selection, iteration) and expression evaluation rules, and why these rules matter for reasoning about program behavior.
Articulate key design goals (readability, writability, reliability/safety, performance, portability) and analyze how particular design decisions improve one goal while constraining another.

Summarize how language paradigm choices (e.g., imperative/procedural, object-oriented, functional) shape how programmers express abstraction and structure solutions, and identify at least two paradigm-driven tradeoffs.
Describe what it means for a language to be precisely specified (informal vs formal specs) and how formalization supports unambiguous interpretation, tooling, and correctness reasoning.

Explain how a programming language specifies legal program forms (syntax), their meaning when executed (semantics), and practical usability concerns (pragmatics), using at least one concrete code-like example to distinguish them.
Describe what types represent, how a type system prevents or detects certain errors, and contrast static vs dynamic typing and strong vs weak checking in terms of safety and flexibility.
Explain why data organization and access patterns drive performance, and identify typical performance considerations (latency, throughput, scalability) that shape storage and retrieval choices.
State why organizations govern data (ownership, stewardship, policy, classification), and summarize how compliance requirements influence collection, retention, and access.
Describe how data moves from capture/creation through storage, processing, sharing, and archival/deletion, and outline the steps that make a repeatable data pipeline.
Explain the primary goals of managing data (e.g., correctness/quality, availability, performance, governance) and how real systems balance these goals via explicit tradeoffs.
Define what it means for data to be accurate, consistent, complete, and timely, and state practices used to preserve integrity (validation, constraints, provenance/lineage).
Explain core privacy/security concerns in data handling (who can access what, leakage risk, misuse), and describe baseline controls such as authentication/authorization and least privilege.
Explain why software changes after delivery (bug fixes, adaptation, enhancement), describe types of maintenance, and connect evolution to cost and long-term quality.
Describe how requirements are elicited and documented, distinguish functional vs. nonfunctional requirements, and state what it means for a specification to be testable and unambiguous.
Present how software design decomposes a system into components/modules with clear interfaces, and how good modularity supports change, reuse, and maintainability.
Explain the core software engineering activities (requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment/operations, and maintenance) and what each produces as an output artifact.
List key quality attributes (e.g., reliability, security, performance, usability, maintainability) and explain that engineering involves prioritizing and trading them off under constraints.
Define verification and validation, outline common testing levels (unit/integration/system/acceptance), and explain how tests provide evidence of correctness relative to requirements.
Define how organizations use patterns to standardize designs (reference architectures, guardrails, review checklists) and document governance practices that ensure consistent adoption.
Explain how patterns are tailored to local constraints and how pattern guidance evolves over time (versioning, deprecation, learning from incidents), while preserving architectural intent.
Explain what an architectural pattern catalog is, how patterns are categorized (e.g., by scope, problem context, and quality attributes), and how teams use catalogs to select consistent solutions.
Describe how multiple patterns can be combined in a single architecture, including how to reason about interactions, conflicts, and how integration choices affect system qualities.
Produce a repeatable method for choosing a pattern for a given set of requirements/constraints, including explicit evaluation criteria (tradeoffs, risks, and suitability to context).
For selected patterns, articulate the primary quality attributes they optimize (e.g., scalability, reliability, security, maintainability) and the common costs/downsides introduced.

Explain how modern web applications separate concerns across client (browser/mobile), server-side application logic, and data storage tiers, and why this separation matters for scalability, maintainability, and security.

Summarize common deployment arrangements (e.g., monolith vs separated frontend/backend, reverse proxy, multi-tier hosting) and describe how environment differences (dev/test/prod) affect configuration and operations.
Explain microservices as an architectural style, including service boundaries, independent deployment, and how multiple services compose to deliver an end-to-end application.
Describe the SPA model, how it differs from multi-page/server-rendered approaches, and the implications for routing, state management, performance, and deployment.

Define what an API is in a web application context and outline how clients communicate with back-end services through HTTP-based interfaces, including typical request/response patterns and responsibilities.

Identify the main quality attributes emphasized in modern web architectures (e.g., performance, scalability, reliability, security, evolvability) and articulate typical tradeoffs when choosing architectural patterns.
Explain why automation is central to cloud-native delivery and describe the purpose of CI/CD pipelines and operational automation for repeatable build, test, release, and rollout.
Define cloud-based and cloud-native applications and clearly distinguish them by their design goals (elasticity, resilience, automation) and typical architectural characteristics.
Explain what containers and images are, what they package (app + dependencies), and why they improve portability and deployment consistency across environments.
Describe decomposing an application into independently deployable services, including how services communicate (APIs) and what benefits/tradeoffs this creates.
Define observability and outline how logs, metrics, and traces are used to understand behavior in distributed systems, diagnose incidents, and support operations.
Summarize core resilience ideas (design for failure, redundancy, graceful degradation) and name the kinds of mechanisms/patterns used to keep services available under faults.

Explain what a cloud mashup is and how applications compose capabilities from multiple clouds/SaaS. Specify the typical integration mechanisms (APIs, events/messaging, data replication/ETL) and where composition logic lives.

Explain how data is placed/replicated across clouds (for locality, compliance, DR) and the tradeoffs that follow (latency, cost, consistency, recovery objectives). Include how data movement is governed and monitored.

Describe what must be standardized and managed across providers to operate reliably (policies, cost controls, observability, incident response, change management). Identify the minimum operational capabilities needed to run hybrid/multicloud solutions safely.

Describe the main hybrid/multicloud architecture shapes (e.g., split by tier, split by service, active-active vs active-passive, edge+cloud) and what problem each pattern solves. Include the key forces (latency, sovereignty, resilience, lock-in) that drive choosing one pattern over another.

Summarize what must be designed to connect and secure workloads across clouds (identity federation, network connectivity, encryption, policy). Explain the trust boundaries and how access control is enforced end-to-end.

State practical strategies to reduce coupling to any one provider (standardized interfaces, containers, infrastructure-as-code, abstraction layers). Distinguish portability of compute/runtime from portability of data and managed services.

Describe why asset inventory and configuration management matter for controlling cyber resources, and specify what a CMDB-like view contains (assets, relationships, owners, baselines) and how it supports change/incident/risk work.

Explain how enterprise IT governance frameworks align IT capabilities with business goals through processes, metrics, and accountability, and summarize how a COBIT-style model structures objectives and management practices.
Define GRC and describe how governance objectives, risk assessment/management, and compliance obligations connect to organizational control selection, assurance activities, and reporting.
Present an ISMS as a management system for continuously improving security, including policy, scope, roles, risk treatment, and audit/continuous improvement cycles (e.g., plan-do-check-act).

Explain IT service management as a framework for delivering and improving IT services, and outline core ITIL-style practices (e.g., incident, problem, change, service request, SLA/monitoring) and how they support operational reliability.
Describe what security controls are (administrative/technical/physical), how they are organized in control catalogs/frameworks, and how organizations map controls to risks and requirements.
